_note: A small curated set of well-documented, independently-dated historical events for context on the timeline page — not an exhaustive historical record, and deliberately not including events (like the Exodus itself) whose date is a live scholarly dispute. Years use astronomical-style signed integers (negative = BC).

events.label: Hammurabi becomes king of Babylon
events.description: The Babylonian king best known for his law code takes the throne — one of the best-documented rulers of the Mesopotamian world Abraham's family came from.

events.label: Egypt's New Kingdom begins
events.description: The Eighteenth Dynasty opens Egypt's most powerful era, the backdrop against which the Exodus narrative is set regardless of which proposed date for it is used.

events.label: Late Bronze Age collapse
events.description: Widespread upheaval across the Eastern Mediterranean and Near East, including the 'Sea Peoples' invasions, reshapes Canaan's political landscape around the time of the judges.

events.label: Phoenician alphabet spreads across the Mediterranean
events.description: The consonantal script that Hebrew itself derives from spreads widely via Phoenician trade networks.

events.label: Battle of Qarqar
events.description: An Assyrian inscription (the Kurkh Monolith) records a coalition that included 'Ahab the Israelite' opposing Shalmaneser III — one of the earliest non-biblical mentions of an Israelite king.

events.label: Fall of Samaria
events.description: The northern kingdom of Israel falls to Assyria under Shalmaneser V and Sargon II, and much of its population is deported.

events.label: Fall of Nineveh
events.description: The Assyrian capital falls to a Babylonian-Median coalition, ending Assyrian dominance of the region.

events.label: Fall of Jerusalem
events.description: Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar II destroys Solomon's Temple and deports much of Judah's population, beginning the exile.

events.label: Cyrus the Great conquers Babylon
events.description: The Persian conquest ends the Babylonian empire and opens the way for exiles to return to Judah.

events.label: Alexander the Great takes the Levant
events.description: Alexander's conquest brings Greek language and culture into the eastern Mediterranean, shaping the world the New Testament was later written into.

events.label: Rededication of the Jerusalem Temple
events.description: After the Maccabean Revolt against Seleucid rule, the Temple is purified and rededicated — the origin of Hanukkah.

events.label: Pompey captures Jerusalem
events.description: Rome absorbs Judea into its sphere as a client territory, beginning the Roman presence that frames the entire New Testament.

events.label: Augustus becomes Rome's first emperor
events.description: The end of the Roman Republic and start of the Pax Romana — the political backdrop for Jesus' birth and the apostles' travels.

events.label: Destruction of the Second Temple
events.description: Roman legions under Titus destroy Jerusalem's Temple after a Jewish revolt — an event the Gospels record Jesus as having foretold.

events.label: Eruption of Mount Vesuvius
events.description: The eruption that buried Pompeii — a precisely-dated fixed point in the same Roman world the apostles wrote to.
